The absence of government security does not justify violence by armed self-defense groups. While understandable as a desperate reaction to fear and abandonment, the decision by private citizens to take up arms and exercise violent power in the name of protection is illegitimate, dangerous, and ultimately destructive to the very security it claims to provide.

The central argument against armed self-defense groups rests on the principle of the rule of law. A functioning society depends on a single, accountable authority holding a monopoly on the legitimate use of force. This principle is not a technicality; it is the foundation of justice. When that monopoly fractures and is replaced by multiple armed factions, each deciding for itself who is guilty, who is a threat, and what punishment is deserved, law ceases to exist. It is replaced by arbitrary power. Self-defense groups, no matter how noble their initial intentions, operate without legal authority, without due process, and without institutional accountability. They become judge, jury, and executioner, violating the fundamental right of every individual to a fair trial and to be presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Furthermore, the absence of the state cannot be cured by actions that make the return of the state even harder. Armed self-defense groups do not fill a security vacuum; they deepen it. Empirical evidence from conflicts around the world shows a clear and predictable pattern. First, a community arms itself against criminals or insurgents. Second, that group must fund itself, sustain itself, and defend its own power, which inevitably leads to extortion, forced recruitment, illegal taxation, and territorial control. Third, rival groups emerge — either aligned with the original enemy or formed by neighboring communities who now feel threatened by the first group. What began as protection becomes a cycle of retaliation and escalation. Violence does not recede; it multiplies and becomes privatized. The community is no longer caught between insecurity and the state, but between insecurity and multiple predatory armed actors.

Proponents of these groups argue that necessity justifies their actions — that when the government fails to protect its people, the people have a inherent right to protect themselves by any means necessary. This argument confuses the right to personal self-defense with the right to wage organized violence. An individual repelling an immediate attack on their own life is fundamentally different from a group organizing, arming itself, mounting patrols, setting up checkpoints, detaining people, and carrying out killings. The former is a personal act of survival in a moment of crisis. The latter is the creation of a parallel armed power structure. Necessity may explain why such groups form, but it does not justify them. A justification would require that their violence produces a stable, just outcome, and it never does.

That is because armed self-defense groups are inherently unaccountable. A state security force, however flawed or absent it may be in the moment, is at least theoretically bound by law, subject to civilian oversight, judicial review, and public pressure for reform. Its failures can be documented, protested, and litigated. An armed self-defense group answers to no one but its own commander. There is no mechanism for a citizen to report its abuses, no court to check its excesses, and no way to disband it once the threat has passed. History is replete with self-defense militias that, once empowered, refused to disarm and became the primary source of human rights abuses, displacement, and extrajudicial killings in their regions.

Finally, legitimizing these groups undermines the long-term project of building real security. Lasting security is not simply the absence of an immediate threat; it is the presence of legitimate institutions capable of protecting rights impartially over time. Every time society accepts that armed civilians can legitimately replace the state, it weakens the incentives and the political pressure needed to reform, rebuild, and hold that state accountable. It sends the message that security is a private commodity to be seized by force, rather than a public good that the state has a duty to provide equally to all.

A state that fails to protect its citizens has failed in its most basic duty, and that failure must be condemned and corrected. But that failure does not transfer the right to commit violence to anyone else. The cure for the absence of lawful authority cannot be the embrace of unlawful violence.
